title: More electrons is not more energy per electron
question: What changes when frequency rises, and what changes when power rises?
recap: In the one-quantum model, frequency sets the maximum electron energy after paying the escape cost. Increasing power at fixed frequency can increase the number emitted without increasing that maximum.
premises: One electron can receive one quantum of energy hν.
Escape requires positive work Φ, with any additional loss nonnegative.
Frequency, work function and yield stay fixed when the power changes.
limitations: In the laboratory the threshold and the straight line follow from the model’s assumptions; they are not experimental proof.
The work function used in a hypothetical example is not a sourced value for a named metal.
Real collection and emission rates require additional material and apparatus assumptions.

overview.text: In the one-quantum model, frequency sets the maximum electron energy after paying the escape cost. Increasing power at fixed frequency can increase the number emitted without increasing that maximum.

full.text: The most energetic electron receives a complete quantum and escapes with the least modeled energy loss. Subtracting the escape work \(\Phi\) gives the maximum kinetic energy, provided emission is energetically allowed.

full.spoken: Maximum kinetic energy equals h frequency minus escape work, with threshold frequency Phi over h.

full.text: For a hypothetical work function of 2 electron volts and a frequency of 600 terahertz, the maximum is about 0.4814 electron volts using modern SI constants. Doubling optical power while retaining that frequency and escape work leaves the maximum unchanged.

Power is energy arriving per second. At fixed frequency, dividing it by \(h\nu\) gives the incoming quantum rate. Under a fixed yield, twice the power can therefore produce twice the electron count per second. Below threshold, negative \(h\nu - \Phi\) is an energy deficit, not a negative kinetic energy of an emitted electron.

full.returnCaption: Return to the slope, threshold, and the distinction between energy and count.

steps.text: Letters: the paper takes the exciting light to consist of energy quanta of size \(\frac{R}{N}\beta\nu\), writes P for the work an electron must do to leave the body (Φ here), and writes ε for the electron's charge. This explanation writes the quantum as hν, with h a later name for Rβ/N.

items: The simplest picture, which the paper assumes occurs: a light quantum gives its whole energy to a single electron. The paper also leaves open that some electrons take up only part of a quantum's energy.
An electron excited inside the body loses part of its kinetic energy before it reaches the surface. The fastest electrons are those excited right at the surface and moving straight out.
Each electron must do a work P, characteristic of the body, to leave it. So the kinetic energy of the fastest electrons is the quantum minus that work: \(\frac{R}{N}\beta\nu-P\).

In the explanatory letters, with hν for the quantum and Φ for P, that is the first half of the formula below. Setting it to zero gives the lowest frequency at which the fastest electron can still escape, the threshold \(\nu_0=\Phi/h\).

steps.spoken: Maximum kinetic energy equals h frequency minus escape work, with threshold frequency Phi over h.

items: Worked case with modern SI constants, for a hypothetical work function of 2 electron volts at a frequency of 600 terahertz: \(h\nu=6.62607\times10^{-34}\times6.00\times10^{14}=3.97564\times10^{-19}\) joule, which divided by \(1.602177\times10^{-19}\) joule per electron volt is 2.4814 electron volts. Subtract 2: the maximum kinetic energy is 0.4814 electron volts.
The threshold for that work function is \(\nu_0=2\) electron volts divided by h, about 484 terahertz.
Below the threshold, \(h\nu-\Phi\) is negative. That is a shortfall of energy: no electron escapes by this route, and there is no negative kinetic energy to report.

The paper's own check, in its letters: charge the body to a positive potential Π that just prevents it from losing electricity. Then Π times the electron's charge ε equals the kinetic energy \(\frac{R}{N}\beta\nu-P\).

Multiply by N: the charge becomes E, the charge of one gram-equivalent of a monovalent ion, and the right side becomes Rβν minus the escape work for that amount of charge. The paper sets that work to zero for an estimate, takes \(E=9{,}6\cdot10^{3}\) in electromagnetic units, \(\nu=1{,}03\cdot10^{15}\), the limit of the solar spectrum toward the ultraviolet, and \(\beta=4{,}866\cdot10^{-11}\).

Then Π = Rβν/E: \(8.31\times10^{7}\times4.866\times10^{-11}\times1.03\times10^{15}/(9.6\times10^{3})=4.34\times10^{8}\) electromagnetic units, with R the standard value of 1905. One volt is \(10^{8}\) of those units, so Π is about 4.34 volts. The page gives 4,3 volts and says the result agrees in order of magnitude with Lenard's.

The paper's further prediction: Π, plotted against the frequency of the exciting light, must be a straight line whose slope does not depend on the substance. In the explanatory letters the slope of \(K_{\mathrm{max}}\) against ν is h for every metal, and only the intercept, set by Φ, changes.

Power sets the count, not the energy of each electron. Optical power is energy per second; divided by hν it gives quanta per second. At 600 terahertz, one milliwatt carries \(2.5\times10^{15}\) quanta per second, and two milliwatts carry twice as many, each still of 2.4814 electron volts.

So, if each quantum gives up its energy independently of all the others, the speeds of the electrons do not depend on the intensity of the light, while the number leaving the body is proportional to it, other things being equal (p. 147). Twice the power can give twice the electrons per second; it cannot raise the maximum energy of one.
The laboratory's straight line follows from the equation it is programmed with. It shows a consequence of the model; only measurements made independently can test the model.

steps.returnCaption: Return to the slope, threshold, and the distinction between energy and count.
Return to the straight line of electron energy against frequency.

margin.text: The source discusses the potential attained by an illuminated body; a later collector apparatus is a distinct arrangement. Later measurements such as Millikan’s 1916 work are not premises available in 1905, and agreement with the energy relation alone does not prove the complete light-quantum picture.
